profile.name: 'upa'upa
profile.tagline: Tahiti's ancestral dance of passionate miming, flutes, and drumming
profile.insight: Outlawed in 1819 by missionaries as immoral, 'upa'upa was danced covertly until 1872 when barefoot dancers overtook the royal gardens while officials danced indoors to a piano.
profile.profile: The 'upa'upa is a traditional dance from Tahiti and the historical predecessor of modern tāmūrē. Traditionally performed in pairs of boys and girls or led by wandering Arioi troupes, it involves passionate, rhythmic movements of the thighs, knees, and loins. Accompanied by voices, flutes, and drums, performances began slowly before accelerating into ecstatic energy that often lasted through the night. Despite fierce bans under colonial and missionary legal codes throughout the nineteenth century, the tradition endured covertly, eventually resurfacing into modern Tahitian cultural life.
profile.profile_long:
The 'upa'upa is an ancestral Tahitian dance whose name served broadly across Tahitian lexicons to denote dance itself. Historically rooted in the performance practices of the Arioi—a sacred brotherhood dedicated to the deities Orotetefa and Urutetefa—the dance was conveyed across islands through dramatic pantomime, singing, and movement. Missionary William Ellis noted in 1829 that upaupa described many spectacles of the Arioi, which began at a measured, slow tempo alongside eccentric gestures before amplifying in intensity toward extreme collective excitement. The performances were sustained across entire nights or days, forming an integral celebration at occasions such as weddings.

European travelers frequently described the choreography in terms of passionate miming and frank sensuality. In 1837, Jacques-Antoine Moerenhout recorded Arioi dances depicting explicit love scenes drawn from mythology. Decades later in 1888, Antoine Mathivet, writing under the pseudonym Monchoisy, depicted the 'upa'upa as a passionate and fiery pantomime where dancers executed rapid, whirling movements of the thighs, knees, and lower back, shaking the entire body alongside inarticulate cries to the accompaniment of monotonous flute and drum rhythms. Danced by mixed pairs of boys and girls, these movements carried expressive and explicit meanings that culminated at times in close embraces.

The arrival of the London Missionary Society in 1797 marked the onset of strict moral surveillance in Tahiti. Under the Pōmare Code of 1819, the 'upa'upa and tattooing were condemned as immoral habits to be severely eradicated, introducing notions of sin to Polynesian festivities. Queen Pōmare IV reinforced these prohibitions in the Tahitian Code of 1842, explicitly banning the dance on the grounds that it caused disorder and moral corruption among youth, and mandating that dance houses be repurposed for prayer, schools, or courts. Despite severe penalties and links to crackdowns on fermented alcohol, dancing persisted covertly in secret venues across the islands.

Colonial administrations oscillated between suppression and partial containment. The French protectorate declared in 1849 that the 'upa'upa remained forbidden except on public feast days, and only without indecent gestures, while the acts of 1853 and 1876 restricted dance permits strictly to chiefs on Saturday evenings. Yet social reality often outpaced decree. In 1872, author Pierre Loti witnessed a royal ball where colonial officials danced to piano music in satin boots inside Queen Pōmare's salon, while outside in the palace gardens, young barefoot women crowned with flowers conducted an immense, night-long 'upa'upa to the sound of drums.

By the early twentieth century, traditional materials began reclaiming public visibility through festivities such as Bastille Day on 14 July. Early transitional attire evolved from Mother Hubbard dresses and ponchos into skirts embellished with raffia by around 1920, developing into the characteristic moré or grass skirt made from hibiscus fibers, alongside bare chests for male performers. The dance underwent formal public revival when Madeleine Mou'a established the dance group Heiva in 1956 under the patronage of the last queen's daughters. With the opening of Faa'a International Airport in 1961 and the rise of tourism, the artistic lineage descending from 'upa'upa returned fully to daily island life.

sections.origins_and_history: The 'upa'upa originated in Tahiti, where the term broadly designated dance in Tahitian dictionaries. Early accounts closely link it to the Arioi, a wandering brotherhood devoted to the sacred pig deities Orotetefa and Urutetefa who traveled between islands staging pantomimes, songs, and dances. Following the 1797 arrival of London Missionary Society missionaries, the dance was condemned, and the Pōmare Code of 1819 formally banned it as immoral. Queen Pōmare IV's Tahitian Code of 1842 renewed the absolute prohibition, ordering that houses used for dancing be converted into public halls for prayer, schooling, or judicial assemblies. French colonial ordinances in 1849, 1853, and 1876 maintained bans or restricted performances under strict permits issued only to chiefs for Saturday nights. Despite suppression, clandestine dancing persisted throughout the nineteenth century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances typically feature groups of paired boys and girls executing movements described in historical accounts as sexually oriented or passionate mime. The dance was traditionally directed by a leader or game master. It begins on a slow, measured cadence accompanied by distinct gestures, gradually accelerating and amplifying in volume and tempo toward a state of high excitement. Dancers perform barefoot, executing rapid, whirling movements concentrated in the thighs, knees, and lower back (reins), accompanied by full-body shaking, articulated posturing, and vocal cries.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for the 'upa'upa relies primarily on human voice, flutes, and drums (tam-tam). Accounts describe the instrumental accompaniment as a driving, rhythmic accompaniment of flute and drum, which supported vocal chants led by a performance master over many continuous hours.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historic Arioi presentations were recorded as occurring with naked performers and onlookers. In 1872, Pierre Loti recorded dancers performing barefoot in royal palace gardens wearing festive gowns and flower crowns. By 1900, dancers incorporated traditional materials into garments resembling ponchos or mother Hubbard dresses. Around 1920, raffia strips were integrated, evolving into the characteristic skirt known as the moré, made from hibiscus fibers. Male dancers were subsequently permitted bare torsos.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance was performed during Arioi touring spectacles, public celebrations, and major social rites such as weddings, where festivities commenced on the eve of the nuptials and extended across multiple days and nights. Beyond theatrical entertainment representing mythological and romantic narratives, the dance functioned as a communal expression of joy and celebration.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical figures include Queen Pōmare IV, who enacted legal bans in 1842; missionary William Ellis, who documented Arioi spectacles in 1829; writer Pierre Loti, who witnessed garden performances in 1872; Antoine Mathivet (Monchoisy), who published detailed movement descriptions in 1888; and Madeleine Mou'a, who founded the troupe Heiva in 1956 under the patronage of Princesses Teri'i and Takau.
sections.regional_variants: The dance flourished in Tahiti and extended across the Society Islands, including the Leeward Islands, which mirrored Tahiti's legal restrictions. In 1912, filmmaker Gaston Méliès recorded a variant performance on Rarotonga in the Cook Islands.
sections.lineage: The 'upa'upa is the historical predecessor of the modern Tahitian tāmūrē and directly informed the repertoire revived by Madeleine Mou'a in the mid-twentieth century.

basic_steps: Stand barefoot with knees softly bent and weight grounded.
Isolate the pelvis and thighs to initiate a rapid, whirling rotation of the knees, thighs, and lower back.
Coordinate full-body shaking while maintaining grounded contact through the feet.
Pair with a partner facing closely, syncing hip and thigh rotations in time with drum cadences.
teaching.rhythm: Begins at a slow, measured tempo and progressively accelerates to a rapid, high-intensity cadence.
teaching.formation: Couples arranged in boy-and-girl pairs, guided by a lead caller or game master.
teaching.level_notes: Requires intense stamina, knee stability, and pelvic articulation to sustain rapid continuous rotation.

music_profile.vocal_style: Chanted verse led by a soloist or leader, escalating from measured delivery to heightened vocalizations and inarticulate cries.
music_profile.musical_form: Continuous progressive acceleration from a slow, measured introduction to an intense, sustained climax.
music_profile.sound_description: A repetitive, hypnotic acoustic texture driven by wooden or skin drums and melodic flute lines, overlaid with rhythmic leader-led chanting that shifts from restrained phrasing into urgent, percussive vocalizations.

movement_profile.posture: Grounded, upright posture danced barefoot with softened knees to facilitate rapid lower-body oscillation.
movement_profile.footwork: Barefoot weight shifts maintaining grounded connection to the earth while supporting rapid knee and thigh movements.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Gestures conveying pantomime and dramatic narrative, supporting the rhythmic movement of the body.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Rapid, whirling movements of the thighs, knees, and loins/reins, accompanied by continuous shaking of the torso and whole body.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Coupled pairs of boys and girls interacting in close proximity within an open communal space or garden.
movement_profile.partnering: Couples dancing opposite one another with expressive, sexually oriented interactions culminating at times in an embrace.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Gradual accelerando from a measured, deliberate pulse to an ecstatic, driving finish.

signature_moves.name: Whirling of the reins
signature_moves.description: Rapid circular and vibrating movements of the pelvis, thighs, and knees.

signature_moves.name: Partner embrace
signature_moves.description: Culminating dramatic hold between paired male and female dancers.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Primarily grounded level; jumps not described in sources.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid stiff knees or isolated upper-body tension that disrupts the natural rotational mechanics of the pelvis.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Dance That Defied the Crown and the Cloth
episode_brief.logline: Banned by missionaries and criminalized by codes, the sensual 'upa'upa survived in Tahiti's shadows before blossoming into modern Polynesian dance.
beats: Open on the Arioi brotherhood arriving by outrigger canoe, igniting an all-night village dance under torchlight.
Recreate the promulgation of the 1819 Pōmare Code, contrasting the written ban with clandestine forest gatherings.
Dramatize Pierre Loti's 1872 account of Queen Pōmare's palace: European officers dancing to piano inside while barefoot dancers take the garden.
Show early 20th-century dancers fashioning hibiscus more skirts and reclaiming public stages during July celebrations.
Highlight Madeleine Mou'a assembling her 1956 troupe to formalize Tahitian dance for the modern era.

lesson_ladder.goal: Establish the barefoot posture and knee elasticity needed for Tahitian movement.
drills: Barefoot parallel stance with deep knee bend and pelvic alignment.
Slow rhythmic weight transfers from foot to foot.
Controlled pelvic tilting without moving the upper torso.

lesson_ladder.goal: Build continuous circular movement in the thighs and lower back.
drills: Slow circular rotations of the hips and knees on a steady beat.
Sustained full-body shaking drills maintaining balance.

lesson_ladder.goal: Integrate coupled miming and dynamic acceleration.
drills: Facing partner drills maintaining eye contact and synchronized hip rotations.
Accelerando runs building tempo from slow cadence to peak speed.
Staged pantomimic gestures resolving into final paired holds.

visual_motifs: Bare feet pressing into volcanic soil and dew-covered grass.
Hibiscus fiber moré skirts swaying in rapid blur.
Contrast between missionary black robes and lush floral crowns.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An authoritative Polynesian cultural historian and dance master who emphasizes precise pelvic mechanics and proud cultural endurance.
episode_brief.music_cue: A solitary wooden flute introducing a slow melody, joined by accelerating skin drum hits that build into an ecstatic, polyrhythmic crescendo.

connections.name: tāmūrē
connections.note: 'Upa'upa is recognized as the direct ancestor of modern tāmūrē.

connections.name: hula
connections.note: Related Polynesian traditional dance form sharing narrative gesturing and rhythmic hip movement.

seniors.seated_version: Perform hip oscillations and upper-body expressive gestures while seated firmly on a sturdy armless chair with feet flat on the floor.
seniors.standing_version: Stand with one hand lightly resting on a ballet barre or chair back, practicing gentle knee flexion and soft pelvic rotations.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Maintain a steady, slow-to-moderate tempo; limit pelvic range of motion to pain-free arcs.
seniors.counts: Perform movements in steady 4-count cycles rather than accelerating.

children.game_version: Play a game where children dance slowly like gentle ocean waves and speed up their knee bounces when the drum beats faster, freezing in place on command.

gaps: Specific metric signatures and BPM tempos are not provided in the historical sources.

claims.text: The 'upa'upa is a traditional dance from Tahiti and is considered the ancestor of the tamure.
claims.quote: ’Upa ’upa (également appelé upa upa, upa-upa ou upaupa) est une danse traditionnelle tahitienne, ancêtre du tamure.

claims.text: Missionary William Ellis recorded in 1829 that upaupa was the name for many Arioi spectacles.
claims.quote: Le missionnaire William Ellis de la London Missionary Society, décrit en 1829 l'upa upa des Arioi : « Upaupa était le nom de beaucoup de spectacles des Areoï ».

claims.text: The dances of the Arioi lasted for the greater part of the night accompanied by chants, flutes, and drums.
claims.quote: Les danses, dirigées par un meneur de jeu, accompagnées de chants, de musique de flûtes et de tambours, duraient la plus grande partie de la nuit.

claims.text: Antoine Mathivet described the dance as rapid and whirling movements of the thighs, knees, and loins accompanied by flute and drum.
claims.quote: Ce sont des mouvements des cuisses, des genoux et des reins, rapides et tournoyants, un secouement de tout l'être, avec des cris inarticulés, sur un accompagnement accompagnement monotone de flûte et de tambour

claims.text: The Pōmare code of 1819 prohibited the 'upa'upa as an immoral habit.
claims.quote: The famous Pōmare code of 1819 declared the ʼupaʼupa (and tattooing in the same line) to be bad and immoral habitudes, severely to be opposed.

claims.text: In 1872, Pierre Loti observed women dancing the upa-upa barefoot to drum sounds in the royal gardens while a ball took place inside.
claims.quote: Elles se préparaient à danser jusqu'au jour, pieds nus et au son du tam-tam, tandis que, chez la reine, on allait danser au piano, en bottines de satin.

claims.text: Madeleine Mou'a organized the dance group Heiva in 1956 under the patronage of the last queen's daughters.
claims.quote: But it was not until 1956 that Madeleine Mouʼa organised a dance group, called the heiva, of which Teriʼi and Takau, daughters of the last queen of Tahiti became patrons.

claims.text: The tradition continues in contemporary times following the revival that integrated descendant dances into daily life.
claims.quote: The opening of Faaʼa International Airport in 1961 and the real start of the tourist industry on Tahiti made all the dances which had come forth from the ʼupaʼupa a part of daily life once more.
